topic.title: Autonomous Hill Development Councils expanded across Ladakh

subtopics.title: Why the AHDC expansion matters
subtopics.summary: The Ladakh Administration has approved Autonomous Hill Development Councils (AHDCs) in all 7 districts after an in-principle agreement with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The move follows Ladakh becoming a Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly in 2019, which makes decentralised local institutions central to governance. Before the expansion, elected councils existed only in Leh and Kargil.

subtopics.title: Legal basis, powers and finances of AHDCs
subtopics.summary: AHDCs function under the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Act and are created through legislation, applying only in Ladakh. Section 3(1) empowers the Government to establish a Council in every district through an official notification. Their powers are mainly administrative and developmental, covering land allotment, district cadre recruitment and promotions, and district development planning. Each AHDC maintains a Council Fund and can levy taxes, fees and other lawful charges for local governance.

subtopics.title: AHDCs versus 6th Schedule councils and Article 371
subtopics.summary: AHDCs and 6th Schedule Autonomous District Councils are both local bodies, but they differ in how they are created, where they apply and what powers they hold. AHDCs are created through legislation and apply only in Ladakh, while 6th Schedule councils have constitutional status under Articles 244(2) and 275(1). Article 371 and Articles 371A to 371J, under Part XXI, provide special safeguards for indigenous culture, customary laws, land rights and local employment.

subtopics.title: Ladakh's profile, demands and 2025 reservation rules
subtopics.summary: Ladakh, known as the Land of High Passes or Maryul, has been administered by the Government of India as a Union Territory since 31 October 2019. Its people demand inclusion under the 6th Schedule, restrictions on land ownership to prevent outsider influx, and a Legislative Assembly. A reservation regulation approved on 2 June 2025 and effective from 3 June 2025 raises the total reservation cap to 85 per cent, with EWS quotas excluded.

quizzes.title: Ladakh and the AHDC expansion
quizzes.passage: Ladakh became a Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly in 2019, so decentralised local institutions have become central to governance. The Ladakh Administration has now approved the setting up of Autonomous Hill Development Councils across the region. Councils in each district will be set up through an official notification issued by the Government. This decision followed an in-principle agreement with the Ministry of Home Affairs, which aims to extend constitutional safeguards under Article 371 to the Union Territory. Until now, elected councils had existed in only a few parts of Ladakh, and the expansion will extend them to all districts. The people of Ladakh have raised several demands, including inclusion under the Sixth Schedule for constitutional protection, restrictions on land ownership to prevent an outside influx, and a Legislative Assembly for representative governance. Article 371 and the articles up to 371J give special constitutional safeguards to certain States and regions, with the aim of protecting indigenous culture, customary laws and local employment. Separately, the Centre has changed the rules for jobs and educational admissions in Ladakh through a new reservation regulation, which came into force shortly after it was approved. The regulation also modifies the reservation law of Jammu and Kashmir as applied to the region. The councils function under a separate Act and their powers are mainly administrative and developmental.

quizzes.title: Powers and finances of AHDCs
quizzes.passage: The Autonomous Hill Development Councils are created through legislation and apply only in Ladakh. Their powers are mainly administrative and developmental. The Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Act gives the government the power to create councils in every district. The Act is therefore the legal basis for the councils and their functions. Every district of Ladakh is to have one such council, and each council works within the powers described above. The councils can exercise authority over land allotment, and they also have authority over district cadre recruitment and promotions. They prepare district development plans for sectors such as health, education, tourism, infrastructure and social welfare. Each council also has financial powers, and it can levy taxes, fees and other lawful charges. The councils do not have judicial authority. This is an important difference from the Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Councils, which can establish village courts under customary tribal laws. The Sixth Schedule councils also have legislative, executive, financial and judicial powers. The Sixth Schedule councils apply to tribal areas in certain northeastern States, while the AHDCs apply only in Ladakh. Ladakh has been administered as a Union Territory since 2019, and it has no Legislative Assembly. Decentralised local institutions are therefore central to how the region is governed.
